title: US Releases New Files On Bigfoot Sightings
excerpt: The U.S. Forest Service released decades of files on reported Bigfoot sightings, including official investigations and eyewitness accounts
content:
The U.S. Forest Service has released a set of historic files detailing reported sightings and tracks of the legendary Bigfoot, adding fresh intrigue to one of America’s most enduring mysteries. These files, made public on the agency’s website, span incidents from the 1940s through the early 2000s and include official investigations and eyewitness accounts across the Pacific Northwest and Montana.

According to a report from The Washington Post, the agency's newly released documents include a 1982 investigation into large footprints found in the Mill Creek Watershed of Washington state’s Umatilla National Forest. Investigators took plaster casts, color photographs, and detailed measurements of the tracks, attempting to preserve the unusual physical evidence for further study.

Another file describes a sighting in Montana in the 1940s, where hunter Leo Kinney and three companions discovered a set of large, human-like tracks near Petty Creek. Kinney later wrote, "At this point we held a conference and decided that we were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was, and though we didn't confess it at this time, in later conversations we found out that we all had a very uneasy feeling and could feel chills running up and down our backs." This account, included in a 1980 document, is among several that detail encounters with unexplained tracks and noises.

A more recent sighting from 2003, documented in Sanders County, Montana, describes hundreds of large footprints in fresh snow outside a sawmill, with prints measuring over 16 inches long and a stride of about five feet. Local resident Bob Mesing, who measured the tracks, said, "I don’t know if I believe in the Bigfoot theory, but the tracks were right there. What else could it be?"

The files also include the perspective of a wildlife biologist, Rodney Johnson, who investigated the 1982 Washington tracks. Johnson concluded that the evidence did not match what would be expected from a 300-pound, two-footed being, citing consistent stride length and unnatural placement of pine needles as possible signs of a hoax.

The U.S. Forest Service has neither confirmed nor denied the existence of Bigfoot, but the recent release of these files follows a broader trend of federal agencies providing public access to previously withheld documents on unexplained phenomena. The agency has also hosted forums, such as the "Bigfoot in Your Backyard" event in California’s Stanislaus National Forest, to discuss local reports.

The files are available to the public through the U.S. Forest Service’s website, and speculation continues about whether additional information will be released in the future.
